title: Contributing
text:
Propose changes through a branch and pull request. Keep changes focused, explain the GeoEpi use case, and update linked templates or resources when a page changes their meaning.
For substantive guidance, include the source or experience behind the recommendation and distinguish a useful group convention from an actual institutional, contractual, security, or scientific requirement. Reviewers should check clarity, accessibility, scientific accuracy, links, and whether the proposed guidance fits the practical GeoEpi operating model.
Render the full site locally with quarto render before opening a pull request. The validation script checks active-page metadata, internal links, templates, and generated output. Do not commit _site/, credentials, tokens, or local IDE state.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text:
The GeoEpi Lab Book is a practical guide for GeoEpi scientists and collaborators. It helps people organize collaborative, computationally intensive geographical epidemiology so that work remains understandable, scientifically defensible, reproducible where access permits, and possible to continue when people or projects change.
It is a living guide, not an administrative compliance manual or a substitute for scientific judgment, data-use agreements, security requirements, funder terms, or institutional policy. GeoEpi conventions are stated as conventions; stronger language is reserved for genuine scientific, security, contractual, or institutional requirements.
The audience includes computational scientists as well as veterinarians, microbiologists, virologists, entomologists, field epidemiologists, wildlife managers, and other domain experts. The organization should remain understandable outside HPC and command-line environments.

title: Templates
text:
These templates are starting points, not a rigid project structure. Copy them into the appropriate project or subproject location, adapt them to the work, and link to the authoritative records.



Template
Use




Project overview
Project context in a future GeoEpi Hub


Data Management Plan
Concise project-level data-management planning


Controlled-data inventory
Minimal project-level inventory of important controlled data


Subproject registry
Future Hub links to canonical subproject repositories


Subproject README
Orientation and reproducibility information in a subproject repository


GeoEpi metadata
Proposed Version 1 portfolio metadata convention for a future .geoepi.yml file



The registry and metadata files intentionally contain portfolio-level information only. subprojects.yml locates the canonical repository; .geoepi.yml reports the subproject’s current portfolio state. Run metadata belongs in the subproject repository and computational storage. Future Hub automation may read these files, but cross-repository automation is not implemented here.

title: Zotero
text:
Zotero is the preferred location for GeoEpi shared literature libraries. Shared collections make references easier for collaborators to find and maintain.
Individuals may use other reference managers for personal workflows. When a paper or source matters to a shared project, add it to the appropriate shared library or record enough citation information in the project’s documentation for others to locate it.

title: GitHub
text:
GeoEpi generally uses GitHub for version-controlled code, documentation, issue and review discussions, collaboration, and canonical subproject repositories. The GeoEpi organization is the normal home for lab-owned subprojects and will eventually host the lab-level Hub.
Repositories may also live in individual accounts, forks, external upstreams, or collaborator-owned organizations. Identify one canonical working repository for each subproject so the future Hub has a stable destination.
GitHub is not a storage system for controlled data, credentials, tokens, or large computational outputs. Use approved storage and computation environments, and link to them from the repository when appropriate.

title: Repository versus Compute
text:
Keep in the subproject repository
Keep in Atlas, Ceres, or other approved compute/storage




README, workflow entry points, code, configuration templates, documentation, schemas, and lightweight manifests
Controlled or large data, intermediate files, caches, temporary objects, logs, and large outputs


Public-source acquisition details and citations
The acquired data and computational working copies


Environment definition or lockfile where practical
Installed environments and execution-specific files


Run metadata needed to identify and reproduce a result
Full run output, scheduler artifacts, and high-volume logs



The boundary is about access, size, and purpose—not a rigid folder layout. A repository can contain small examples and test fixtures. It should not contain credentials, tokens, controlled data, or large computational outputs.
Run-level details remain with the subproject and/or computational storage: environment versions, package versions, model parameters, random seeds, replicates, SLURM job IDs, input manifests, configuration, logs, output manifests, and validation details. The Hub should not duplicate them.

title: Computing & Repositories
text:
GeoEpi commonly separates the durable scientific record from the computational workspace:

GitHub holds code, version control, documentation, collaboration, and subproject repositories.
Atlas and Ceres hold approved large or controlled data, intermediate data, HPC execution, logs, temporary objects, and large outputs.
The repository versus compute boundary explains what to record in each place.

The exact storage and access arrangement depends on the project, data agreements, and institutional systems. Record the authoritative location clearly and keep project context accessible to collaborators who may not have SCINet or HPC access.

title: Controlled-Data Inventory
text:
The future Hub should inventory project data whose stewardship matters, such as surveillance or case detections, field-collected data, genomic or sample data, facility or premises-level data, diagnostic data, partner-provided datasets, restricted extracts, and other controlled or governed data.
The inventory is a map, not a copy of the data. Do not store controlled data in GitHub. For each important data asset, record a stable ID, name and description, provider, project steward, authoritative storage location, access or restriction level, applicable agreement or limitation, relevant subprojects, and current status or notes.
Public analytical sources do not need to be cataloged exhaustively in the Hub. Sources such as ERA5, MODIS, administrative boundaries, census data, public host or livestock surfaces, roads, and night lights should normally be documented by the subproject repository that acquires or uses them.
Use the controlled-data inventory template for a minimal starting point. The project DMP explains how the project plans to manage data; the inventory records what is actually present.

title: Data Management
text:
GeoEpi uses three related records for three different questions:







Record
Question it answers




Project DMP
How will this project manage its data?


Controlled-data inventory
What important controlled or project-generated data actually exist?


Subproject analytical provenance
Exactly which data did this analysis use, and how were they processed?



The project DMP and controlled-data inventory belong with project context in the Hub. Analytical provenance belongs with the subproject that acquires or uses the data. Do not collapse these into one giant record, and do not require every subproject to maintain a separate formal DMP.
The guiding idea is as open as possible and as restricted as necessary. Controlled, proprietary, partner-provided, sensitive, contractual, or otherwise restricted data may remain restricted.
Continue to Project DMPs, Controlled data, or Analytical provenance.

title: Projects and Subprojects
text:
A project is a broad scientific or operational objective. It may include several scientists, controlled or partner-provided data, multiple analytical workstreams, and several products.
A subproject is an independently understandable and executable workstream. Examples include NWS climate acquisition, a Bayesian risk model, a spread simulation, genomics, or a dashboard.
The useful rule is approximately:
This is not the same as “one scientist = one repository.” A scientist may contribute to several subprojects, and a subproject may involve several scientists. Each subproject has one designated canonical working repository, even when forks, upstream repositories, or collaborator-owned repositories also exist.

title: Projects and Subprojects
text:
Where information belongs

Project level: objective, scope, roles, decisions, milestones, controlled-data stewardship, and products.
Subproject level: scientific implementation, workflow entry points, public data acquisition, code, analytical provenance, and reproducibility notes.
Run level: exact configuration and execution records for a particular analysis or computational run.

Use the subproject README template and proposed Version 1 .geoepi.yml template when setting up a repository. The metadata file is a small future convention, not a replacement for the README or run records.

title: Projects and Subprojects
text:
Stable identifiers
project_id and subproject_id are stable machine-readable identifiers. Use lowercase, short but understandable, hyphen-separated ASCII names with no spaces. Do not add dates unless a date is genuinely part of the scientific identity, and do not change an ID merely because a project title changes.
For example:
project_id: nws-risk
subproject_id: nws-bayes-risk
subproject_id: nws-climate-acquisition
Stable IDs may eventually connect Hub directory names, Hub registries, .geoepi.yml, GitHub Actions, analytical metadata, and computational paths where appropriate. GeoEpi is not prescribing a run ID convention yet.

title: Projects and Subprojects
How GeoEpi Organizes Work
text: GeoEpi organizes work as a network rather than a single directory. The lab-level Hub provides the project portfolio and shared context. Each coherent analytical workstream has a canonical subproject repository. Computation and large data live in the appropriate computational environment, and accepted outputs move into project synthesis and dissemination systems.

title: How GeoEpi Organizes Work
text:
The vocabulary



Term
Meaning




GeoEpi Hub
The future single lab-level project-management and portfolio repository in the GeoEpi GitHub organization. It holds project context and coordination.


Project
A broad scientific or operational objective with people, data, analytical workstreams, and products.


Subproject
One independently understandable and executable analytical, software, data-acquisition, modeling, genomic, dashboard, or related workstream.


Repository
The canonical Git repository for a subproject’s scientific implementation.


Run
One computational execution and its parameters, environment, inputs, logs, outputs, and validation details.


Product
A manuscript, report, dashboard, released dataset, operational output, or other accepted scientific result.



The hierarchy is GeoEpi Hub → Project → Subproject → Run. Products may integrate results from one or more subprojects.
An individual folder in the GeoEpi Hub is a project entry. The Hub is the portfolio and shared context; a project entry is one project within it.
Read the GeoEpi Hub architecture, project and subproject guidance, and repository guidance for practical decisions.
The Hub is planned for a future phase. This refactor documents the architecture and provides templates; it does not create the Hub or implement cross-repository automation.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text: The GeoEpi Lab Book helps scientists and collaborators organize work that combines geography, epidemiology, ecology, biology, data, and computation. It is a practical living guide for improving scientific quality, reproducibility, continuity, and efficiency.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text:
The basic model
A GeoEpi project is a network of linked analytical subprojects, data assets, computational work, and scientific products—not a single repository or directory.





flowchart TD
    H[GeoEpi Hub] --> P1[Project A]
    H --> P2[Project B]
    P1 --> R1[Subproject repository]
    P1 --> R2[Subproject repository]
    P2 --> R3[Subproject repository]
    R1 --> C[Atlas / Ceres]
    R2 --> C
    R3 --> C
    R1 --> S[Synthesis and products]
    R2 --> S
    R3 --> S
    S --> M[Manuscript]
    S --> D[Dashboard or report]
    S --> O[Released data or product]







The GeoEpi Hub holds project context and coordination.
A subproject repository holds the scientific implementation and analytical provenance for one coherent workstream.
Atlas and Ceres hold approved large or controlled data and computational work.
Products include manuscripts, reports, dashboards, released data, and other accepted outputs.

Run-level details—parameters, environments, random seeds, job IDs, logs, manifests, and outputs—stay with the subproject and its computational storage. They do not belong in the Hub.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
section: Start with the question you have
text:
Start with the question you have

Start Here gives the shortest path for a new or inherited project.
How GeoEpi organizes work explains Hub, project, subproject, repository, and run.
Data management separates the project DMP, controlled-data inventory, and analytical provenance.
Computing and repositories explains what belongs on GitHub versus Atlas or Ceres.
Tools and collaboration describes the group’s common working tools.
Templates provides a small set of reusable starting points.

title: Start Here
text: If you are new to a project, start with its parent project in the GeoEpi Hub. The Hub is the place to understand why the project exists, who is involved, what data stewardship matters, and what the project is expected to produce.

text:
The quick distinction







Place
Use it for




GeoEpi Hub
Project context, coordination, decisions, people, milestones, products, and project-level data stewardship


Subproject repository
Code, documentation, analytical inputs, workflow entry points, provenance, and reproducible implementation

Continue to How GeoEpi organizes work when you need to decide where a project or subproject belongs.

title: GeoEpi Hub
text:
GeoEpi will ultimately maintain one lab-level GeoEpi Hub, normally within the geoepi GitHub organization. The GeoEpi Hub is a shared project-management and portfolio repository. It is not an analysis repository and not an HPC run registry.
Information stored directly in the GeoEpi Hub must be appropriate for everyone who has access to that repository. GitHub repository permissions generally do not provide project-folder-specific access control.

title: GeoEpi Hub
GeoEpi Hub
text:
Minimal project-entry structure
Keep the project entry deliberately small:
projects/
  nws-risk/
    README.md
    decisions.md
    data/
      data-management-plan.md
      controlled-data-inventory.csv
    subprojects.yml
    products.yml
Complex projects may add scope.md, people.md, milestones.md, or deliverables.md, but these are not required as separate files when the project README already communicates the information clearly. Use the project overview template to shape a future project entry.

title: GeoEpi Hub
text:
Access boundary
The GeoEpi Hub should not contain controlled data themselves, credentials or tokens, sensitive personnel information, confidential partner communications, restricted agreements when repository access is too broad, or sensitive operational information inappropriate for all Hub users.
Where restricted material exists, record its existence and authoritative approved location when appropriate. The Hub records where restricted resources belong; it does not need to contain the restricted resources themselves. Do not invent institutional security classifications; follow the applicable agreement, security guidance, and institutional direction.

title: GeoEpi Hub
text:
Human-maintained and generated content
The intended future division is:
projects/                         human-maintained project records
project subprojects.yml files     human-maintained canonical pointers
generated/                         automation-owned portfolio summaries
Future files beneath generated/ should not normally be edited manually. Examples might include generated/subproject-status.csv, generated/portfolio-summary.yml, and generated/stale-subprojects.csv. These are examples only; they are not created in this phase.
Future automation should follow the principle: Synchronize project state, not project content.
Run parameters, package versions, random seeds, SLURM job IDs, input manifests, logs, output manifests, and detailed analytical decisions stay in the subproject repository or computational storage. The GeoEpi Hub points to canonical repositories and project context; it does not duplicate every run.

title: Canonical Repositories
text:
GeoEpi subproject repositories will normally be located in the GeoEpi GitHub organization, but the operating model also permits repositories in individual GitHub accounts, forks, external upstreams, and collaborator-owned organizations.
Every subproject should identify one canonical working repository. The future Hub points to that repository. It does not need to catalog every fork, mirror, or temporary branch.

title: Project Data Management Plans
text:
A Data Management Plan is a project-level plan for how data will be generated, managed, protected, shared, and preserved. It is not a run record and does not need to be duplicated for every subproject.
For the conceptual structure, GeoEpi follows the six categories described by the USDA National Agricultural Library, with ICPSR data-management guidance as a secondary reference:

Expected data types — what the project will collect, create, receive, or reuse, including useful metadata.
Data formats and standards — formats, schemas, data dictionaries, and community standards.
Data storage and preservation — working locations, authoritative copies, backup/recovery, retention, and long-term preservation.
Data sharing, protection, and public access — access levels, restrictions, agreements, licenses, embargoes, and release plans.
Roles and responsibilities — who manages data, maintains access, handles transitions, and supplies needed resources.
Monitoring and review/reporting — how implementation, sharing, and changes will be reviewed and reported.

Keep the plan specific enough to guide the project, but proportional to its data and risks. Review it when the project’s data, agreements, storage, people, or products change. Include a review date and responsible person.
Start with the DMP template. The NAL page describes USDA and ARS contexts; GeoEpi uses it here as the primary conceptual source and does not infer additional USDA or institutional requirements from it.

Atlas and Ceres
Tools & Collaboration
text:
GeoEpi uses several complementary systems. The right tool depends on the work and the collaborators; no single programming language or interface is mandatory.







Tool
Common GeoEpi role




GitHub and the GeoEpi organization
Code, version control, documentation, collaboration, subproject repositories, and the future Lab Hub


SCINet, Atlas, and Ceres
Large or controlled data, computation, and HPC


OSF
Collaborator-accessible research objects, data sharing, or project resources where appropriate


Overleaf and LaTeX
Collaborative manuscripts and technical documents, especially equations and complex scientific formatting


Zotero
Shared GeoEpi literature libraries; individuals may use other managers for personal workflows


Quarto and GitHub Pages
Reproducible reports, technical documentation, websites, and notebooks


R
A commonly used language in GeoEpi workflows and examples, alongside other appropriate tools



Read the pages for GitHub, Overleaf, Zotero, and OSF.

title: Overleaf and LaTeX
text:
GeoEpi generally prefers Overleaf and LaTeX for collaborative manuscripts and technical documents, particularly when a document contains equations, complex scientific formatting, or a publisher-specific LaTeX workflow.
Keep the manuscript’s source, references, figures, review decisions, and release relationship understandable to the project team. Link the document to the relevant project and subproject repositories or Hub records, while following collaborator and publisher access requirements.

title: OSF
text:
OSF can provide a collaborator-accessible location for research objects, project resources, or data sharing when it fits the project and access requirements. It complements GitHub and computational storage; it does not replace the canonical subproject repository or the project Hub.
Choose the location that matches the data, agreement, preservation, and collaboration needs. Restricted or sensitive data should remain in an approved restricted system.

title: Resources
text: These links are useful starting points, not a policy catalog. Check the source page, current version, license, access conditions, and fit for your project before relying on a resource.

title: Resources
text:
Data management

USDA National Agricultural Library: Data Management Planning — primary conceptual source for the six-part project DMP structure used in this Lab Book.
ICPSR: Share & Manage Data — secondary practical guidance on managing, documenting, sharing, and preserving research data.
Ag Data Commons — a USDA data discovery and repository resource where appropriate.

title: Resources
text:
GeoEpi tools and working systems

SCINet — USDA scientific computing and storage context, including Atlas and Ceres.
GitHub — GeoEpi organization and subproject repositories.
Quarto — reproducible reports, websites, notebooks, and technical documentation.
Overleaf — collaborative LaTeX documents and manuscripts.
Zotero — shared literature management.
OSF — collaborator-accessible research objects and project resources where appropriate.

The GeoEpi tools page explains the role of each system and the boundaries between them.

title: Resources
text:
Online guides for analytical work
These online books, manuals, and course materials are useful references for analytical work commonly encountered in GeoEpi. They are learning resources, not prescribed methods; use the approach appropriate to the scientific question and data.

Ecology, population biology, and forecasting

Primer of Ecology - ecological modeling and quantitative population concepts.
Quantitative Biology - quantitative biology concepts and worked examples.
A Practical Guide to Ecosystem Forecasting - ecological forecasting workflows.
Forecasting: Principles and Practice - forecasting workflows with the forecast package in R.



Spatial analysis and geocomputation

Spatial Data Science - spatial analysis workflows and concepts.
R | Intro to GIS and Spatial Analysis - introductory GIS and spatial analysis in R.
Spatial Data Processing with R - spatial data processing workflows in R.
Geocomputation with R - geocomputation and spatial data science in R.



Statistics and comparative methods

Rethinking - Bayesian statistical modeling and model reasoning.
Comparative Methods - comparative methods and phylogenetic analysis concepts.
Non-Gaussian Models in Stan - using CmdStanR interface to fit Stan models.
Prior Choice Recommendations - Choosing Bayesian priors, especially in Stan.



Population, landscape, and computational genetics

Landscape Genetic Data Analysis with R - population and landscape genetic analysis.
Applied Population Genetics - applied population genetics workflows.
Molecular Epi in R - molecular epidemiology analysis in R.
Computational Genomics Manual - computational genomics methods and implementation.



Epidemiology

The Epidemiologist R Handbook - applied epidemiological analysis in R.



Network analysis

Network Analysis in R - network methods and implementation in R.
Network Analysis: Integrating Social Network Theory, Method, and Application with R - network theory and applied analysis in R.



Causal analysis

Causal Inference in R - answering causal questions using R.



Integrated Laplace Approximation

Dynamic Time Series Models using R-INLA - use of an approximate Bayesian methods with R-INLA for dynamic modeling of time series.
Spatial SPDE Models - spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA.



Software development, HPCs, and computer science

Applied HPC with R - applied HPC with R is a collection of talks and lectures about speeding up your R code parallel computing and other resources.
R Packages (2e) - 2nd edition of R Packages by Hadley Wickham. Functional programing and paackage design.

title: How to use this site
text:
Use the top navigation to answer practical questions:

Start with Start Here if you are joining, starting, or recovering work.
Use How GeoEpi organizes work to place a project, subproject, or repository.
Use Data Management for project data stewardship and analysis-specific provenance.
Use Computing & Repositories for GitHub, Atlas, Ceres, and run-level records.
Use Tools & Collaboration for common GeoEpi tools.
Copy a starting point from Templates.
Check Resources for external guidance.

Projects differ. Adapt the templates to the work, record important deviations, and link to the authoritative location of the information. Detailed scientific and domain guidance will be developed separately; the archived material is retained for that future work.
